svg.title: Browser and mobile boundaries, and where each one stops
svg.desc: Three panels. Browser isolation: the same-origin policy as the default boundary, CORS as the server-controlled relaxation of it, and CSP with SRI as added constraints on what may execute. Mobile platform isolation: Android per-app UIDs with SELinux, the iOS sandbox where all third-party apps run as the user mobile, and key storage in the Android Keystore backed by a TEE or StrongBox and in the iOS Keychain with keys protected by the Secure Enclave rather than stored inside it. Client-side hardening: response headers, never storing session tokens in localStorage, and reverse-engineering defenses that raise cost without being a boundary.
svg.text: The client enforces boundaries it does not own
The browser and the mobile OS provide the boundaries. The application configures them — and nothing the client checks is a security decision.
BROWSER — THE ORIGIN MODEL
Scheme, host, and port define the boundary
SOP restricts reading across origins, not sending — which is
exactly why CSRF exists as a separate class.
CORS is the server opting in to being readable by a named origin.
CSP constrains what may execute; SRI pins third-party files.
COOP, COEP, and CORP isolate the browsing context.
Reflecting the Origin header with credentials allowed trusts everyone.
MOBILE — TWO DIFFERENT ISOLATION MODELS
Same guarantee, different mechanism
Android — a distinct Linux UID per app, enforced by the kernel, plus
a per-app SELinux domain since Android 9 for API 28 and above.
iOS — no per-app UID. All third-party apps run as the user
mobile, isolated by a mandatory sandbox profile and a randomly
assigned home directory, on a read-only system partition.
Neither platform uses a TPM — that is a PC-platform specification.
KEY STORAGE — THE PROPERTY WORTH WANTING IS A NON-EXPORTABLE KEY
Android Keystore — keys generated and used inside a TEE, or inside StrongBox, which requires its own CPU, secure storage,
a true random number generator, a secure timer, and tamper resistance. StrongBox is slower and supports fewer algorithms.
iOS Keychain — an encrypted SQLite database on the file system. Per-item secret keys require a round trip through the Secure
Enclave; the keychain is protected by the Secure Enclave rather than stored inside it. Keys can also be generated in the Enclave.
Never store a session token in localStorage — any script in the origin reads it, so one XSS is total theft. An HttpOnly cookie is unreadable by script.
Root and jailbreak detection, anti-debugging, and obfuscation raise cost. They are not a boundary — re-decide everything on the server.
